expr-a1-001: In French you have hunger, with {avoir}: {j'ai faim}, never {je suis faim}.
expr-a1-002: Just like hunger: you have thirst. {J'ai soif} works anywhere, with friends or strangers.
expr-a1-003: French says you "have reason": {avoir raison}. The opposite also takes {avoir}: {avoir tort}, to be wrong.
expr-a1m1-001: Men write {enchanté}, women write {enchantée}, and they sound the same.
expr-a1m1-003: A common answer to {ça va ?}. Like "not bad" in English, it means "pretty good".
expr-a1m1-004: It's casual but everywhere: friends, coworkers, even waiters. In formal settings, pick something else.
expr-a1m1-005: Use it to answer a {pardon !} or a request for help, with anyone.
expr-a1m2-001: Said at the table, right before eating. To answer: {merci, vous aussi !} or {toi aussi !}
expr-a1m2-002: It's the call that the meal is ready, very much a family thing: {les enfants, à table !}
expr-a1m2-003: Only for someone you'll see again the same day. For another day, say {à demain} or {à bientôt}.
expr-a1m2-004: The go-to reply when someone calls you: {oui, tout de suite !} Don't mix it up with {tout à l'heure}.
expr-a1m2-005: A daytime goodbye you can say to anyone, even the cashier. In the evening, switch to {bonne soirée}.
expr-a1m3-001: It uses {vous}, so it's the polite way to stop a stranger. With friends, say {excuse-moi}.
expr-a1m3-002: A politer {de rien}, with {vous}. With friends: {je t'en prie}. It can also mean "go ahead" or "after you".
expr-a1m3-003: For the total at the checkout. To ask the price of just one thing, say {c'est combien ?}
expr-a1m3-004: Watch the {trop}: it means "too much". If it's just "very expensive", say {c'est très cher}.
expr-a1m3-005: What the seller asks at the market or bakery. If you're done, answer {c'est tout, merci}.
expr-a1m4-002: For anyone leaving on a trip. Before a holiday, French also says {bonnes vacances !}
expr-a1m4-003: For anyone sick or recovering. With friends, you can also say {soigne-toi bien !}
expr-a1m4-004: This one uses {tu}, for friends and family. With people you don't know, say {à vos souhaits !}
expr-a1m4-005: {Quel temps !} is an exclamation, not a question. It's usually a complaint, but tone can flip it.
expr-a1m5-001: This is the {tu} version, for people you're close to. For a more formal guest: {faites comme chez vous}.
expr-a1m5-002: {Chez} already means "at the home of": {chez moi}, {chez toi}, {chez Marie}. No need for {maison}.
expr-a1m5-003: On its own, {bienvenue !} stays the same for anyone. To welcome someone home: {bienvenue chez moi}.
expr-a1m5-004: To compliment clothes, a color or a haircut, with {tu}. With someone you call {vous}: {ça vous va bien}.
expr-a1m5-005: Careful: the thing does the pleasing, not you. To say you like it, answer {oui, ça me plaît !}
expr-a1m6-001: The Friday goodbye at work or school. Note the French spelling: {week-end}, with a hyphen.
expr-a1m6-002: It's for goodbyes; when you arrive, it's {bonsoir}. At bedtime, it's {bonne nuit}.
expr-a1m6-003: {C'est parti !} kicks things off with energy: a game, a trip, a lesson. Fine with anyone.
expr-a1m6-004: Casual, for friends, right after {salut}. Nothing to report? Just say {rien de spécial}.
expr-a1m6-005: What you say when you run into someone after ages. To give the length: {ça fait deux ans}.
expr-a2-001: Everyday French, fine even with coworkers. The helper {donne un coup de main}: {tu me donnes un coup de main ?}
expr-a2-002: The nerves right before an exam, a show, an interview, not fear in general. It's {j'ai le trac}.
expr-a2-003: It takes {faire}: {je fais la grasse matinée}. The classic Sunday plan, fine to say to anyone.
expr-lote1-001: Meaning "anything", it's neutral. Meaning "nonsense", it's blunt: {tu dis n'importe quoi !} is for friends.
expr-lote1-002: Don't drop the {en}: {j'en ai marre}. Add what with {de}: {j'en ai marre du bruit}. It's casual.
expr-lote1-015: Fine anywhere, even at work. Say who with {à}: {passer un coup de fil à Paul}.
expr-lote1-016: Like British English, French uses {queue} for a line: {je fais la queue}, with {faire}.
expr-lote1-017: It takes {de} + verb: {j'ai hâte de partir}. Despite looking like "haste", it's not about hurrying.
expr-lote2-013: It usually goes with {passer}: {j'ai passé une nuit blanche}. Party, work or worry, any reason counts.
expr-lote3-006: Casual, for things and situations. About a person it's a put-down: {il est nul en maths}, hopeless at math.
expr-lote3-007: For any good news: {c'est génial !} It works for people too: {il est génial}, "he's amazing".
expr-lote3-008: It's the polite stand-in for a swear word, fine in front of kids, like "darn". Often just {mince !}
expr-lote3-012: Note the {de}, where English says "with": {tomber amoureux de Julie}. In the past it takes {être}: {il est tombé}.
expr-lote4-001: Where English says "pretend that", French prefers {de} + verb: {il fait semblant de dormir}.
expr-lote4-002: Very common in the negative, to apologize: {je n'ai pas fait exprès}. The final {s} is silent.
expr-001: It's casual and takes {avoir}: {j'ai la gueule de bois}. For a person's face, {gueule} is rude.
expr-002: The annoyed person goes before the verb: {tu me casses les pieds}. Casual, but no swear word.
expr-003: The person stood up goes before the verb: {il m'a posé un lapin}. Casual, for a date or any plan.
expr-lote1-003: Very common among friends, but crude: never with your boss or strangers. Neutral: {ça m'est égal}.
expr-lote1-004: Vulgar: only with people you're very close to, ideally about yourself: {je suis dans la merde}.
expr-lote1-005: Very common in everyday speech. It can also mean a place is sketchy: {ce quartier craint}.
expr-lote1-006: It takes {de} + verb: {j'ai la flemme de cuisiner}. Very casual, so not something to tell your boss.
expr-lote1-007: Works for good or bad surprises, just like {c'est fou}. Casual, for friends.
expr-lote1-008: As an order it's aggressive: {foutez le camp !} {Je fous le camp} just means "I'm leaving", but crudely.
expr-lote1-009: It truly offends; only among close friends, joking. Not crude, but still curt: {tais-toi}.
expr-lote1-010: It's vulgar: you'll mostly hear {ça me fait chier}. Avoid it with anyone you don't know well.
expr-lote1-011: Very common as advice to calm someone down: {ne te prends pas la tête}. Casual.
expr-lote1-012: It's all in the ironic tone, like "yeah, right": {tu parles !} isn't asking anyone to talk.
expr-lote1-013: Like "a piece of cake", but with {du}, never {un}. The negative is common too: {ce n'est pas du gâteau}.
expr-lote1-014: {Cafard} also means cockroach, but here it's a passing sadness. It takes {avoir}: {j'ai le cafard}.
expr-lote2-001: It's aggressive, the language of a fight. Elsewhere, the verb {dégager} means "to clear".
expr-lote2-002: Careful: {se casser} can also mean to break, as in {le verre s'est cassé}. Context tells you.
expr-lote2-003: It's vulgar but heard a lot. About a person it's insulting: {il est chiant}. Avoid it with strangers.
expr-lote2-004: Like {avoir peur}, it takes {avoir} and {de}: {j'ai la trouille de prendre l'avion}. Casual.
expr-lote2-005: It's casual and agrees with the speaker: a woman says {je suis crevée}. On a tire, {crevé} means flat.
expr-lote2-006: Party slang, close friends only. The neutral word is {ivre}. A woman says {je suis bourrée}.
expr-lote2-007: Slang, with friends or family. Like {avoir faim}, it takes {avoir}: {j'ai la dalle}.
expr-lote2-008: Slang, close friends only: a softened form of a cruder phrase. Note the {me}: {tu me casses les bonbons}.
expr-lote2-009: Informal, among friends, when a story sounds too good to be true. With {vous}: {arrêtez votre char}.
expr-lote2-010: Informal and very common. In the past tense {tomber} takes {être}: {elle est tombée dans les pommes}.
expr-lote2-011: For riddles and guessing games, among friends. {Sa} changes with the person: {je donne ma langue au chat}.
expr-lote2-012: English pays an arm and a leg; French pays {les yeux de la tête}. Fine in any conversation.
expr-lote2-014: English throws in the towel, French throws the sponge: {jeter l'éponge}. Both come from boxing.
expr-lote2-015: Same picture as in English, but with {avoir}: {il a la tête dans les nuages}. Fine in any setting.
expr-lote2-016: A compliment that works anywhere. Watch the preposition: the heart is {sur la main}, "on" the hand.
expr-lote3-001: Very common in everyday talk, with anyone. To say the opposite: {ça ne vaut pas le coup}.
expr-lote3-002: Informal, for small mishaps like missing a bus. For truly sad news, {pas de bol} sounds far too light.
expr-lote3-003: Note the {du}: {il a du bol}. For bad luck it's {pas de bol}. Both are informal, among friends.
expr-lote3-004: Casual; in formal settings, {faites attention}. Careful: {faire une gaffe}, with {une}, means to make a blunder.
expr-lote3-005: Informal. It's a {se} verb, so the past takes {être}: {je me suis planté}, or {plantée} for a woman.
expr-lote3-009: Informal. It agrees with whoever's laughing: a woman says {j'étais morte de rire}. In texts it's {mdr}.
expr-lote3-010: Informal, and it works for people, places or things: {elle est au top}, {ce restaurant est au top}.
expr-lote3-011: No article, just like "lose patience" in English: {je perds patience}. Fine in any setting, formal or not.
expr-lote3-013: It's rude, even with no swear word: the {la} is the mouth. Still blunt but milder: {tais-toi}.
expr-lote3-014: It sounds angry and rude, so only with people you're very close to. Politer: {laisse-moi tranquille}.
expr-lote3-015: Slang for reacting to something outrageous, close friends only. Milder: {tu te moques de moi ?}
expr-lote3-016: It can shock, so never with strangers. It also means a big mess: {c'est le bordel ici}.
expr-lote3-017: It covers anger, shock, even awe, but it's crude: recognize {putain} and never use it with strangers.
expr-lote3-018: A real insult that can start a fight: best to just recognize it. For a woman it becomes {espèce de conne}.
expr-lote3-019: A strong insult, best kept for recognizing. It's masculine; for a woman French uses {connasse}.
expr-lote4-003: Same image as in English, and fine anywhere, even at work: {il faut tourner la page}.
expr-lote4-004: Nothing to do with wanting. Don't drop the {en}: {je t'en veux} means "I hold it against you".
expr-lote4-005: Informal and a bit crude: skip it at work. A milder version is {c'est fichu}.
expr-lote4-006: Casual and very common. It agrees with the speaker: a woman says {je suis fauchée}.
expr-lote4-007: Not "have the balls" (be brave): {j'ai les boules} means you're gutted. Very casual, friends only.
expr-lote4-008: Casual, and always with {avoir} and {la}: {j'ai la pêche}. Nobody's talking fruit here, it's all energy.
expr-lote4-009: A casual verb, conjugated like {parler}: {j'ai galéré}. For a hard task, say {c'est la galère}.
expr-lote4-010: {Le fric} is slang for {l'argent}: fine with friends, but at a job interview or the bank, stick to {argent}.
expr-lote4-011: Vulgar and hurtful: understand it, but don't say it. Without the swear word, French says {tu m'embêtes}.
expr-lote4-020: Casual, for friends. It agrees with the person: {il est cinglé}, {elle est cinglée}.
expr-b2-001: Like "dot the i's", but often firmer, close to "set the record straight": {mettre les points sur les i}.
expr-b2-002: Casual and a bit teasing. Note the {un}: it's always {un poil}, a single hair, never {des poils}.
expr-b2-003: Always negative, and watch the {y}: {tu n'y vas pas de main morte !}, {il n'y est pas allé de main morte}.
expr-lote1-018: Casual and ironic, for people you know well. The French sometimes pull down an eyelid while saying {mon œil !}
expr-lote1-019: Close to "get on your high horse", and the possessive changes too: {je monte sur mes grands chevaux}.
expr-lote1-020: Casual and very common after lunch, like "I'm crashing". It takes {avoir} and {un}: {j'ai un coup de barre}.
expr-lote2-017: Casual and good-humored, much softer than {être bourré}. Use it to tease, not to insult.
expr-lote2-018: Cheekier than {coûter les yeux de la tête}, the everyday version. Keep {la peau des fesses} for friends.
expr-lote2-019: Casual. Don't drop the {en}: {ne va pas en faire tout un fromage !} In French, the fuss becomes a cheese.
expr-lote2-020: Fine in any setting. {Jaune} never changes, and in the past it's {il a ri jaune}.
expr-lote3-020: Casual, for someone way off base. Often with {complètement} before it: {il est complètement à côté}.
expr-lote4-012: {Va te faire voir} is rude and ends the talk in anger. It softens a swear, but avoid it, even with friends.
expr-lote4-013: {La gueule} is an animal's mouth, so it sounds crude. Fine with friends; with your boss, say {faire la tête}.
expr-lote4-014: Very crude because of {foutre}: friends only. The possessive changes: {ils se foutent de notre gueule}.
expr-lote4-015: It takes {être} and {les}: {je suis sur les nerfs}. Casual, but very natural in everyday talk.
expr-lote4-016: Like "it's pouring", it only works with {il}: {il pleut des cordes}, never {ça pleut}.
expr-lote4-017: Casual and positive: always {le paquet}, singular. In the past: {il a mis le paquet}.
expr-lote4-018: Casual, mostly about cars and bikes: {la caisse} is slang for a car. With friends, plain {à fond} works too.
expr-lote4-019: Casual and always negative. In speech, the {ne} often drops: {ça casse pas des briques}.
